sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Most existing agentic reinforcement learning methods assume single-session trajectories, where interaction proceeds within one continuously accumulated context. However, agentic techniques such as context compaction and subagent forking may produce trajectories spanning multiple sessions, creating a mismatch between the single-session training assumption and inference-time execution. Therefore, we introduce Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, a more general setting that supports an arbitrary number of sessions within a trajectory. Under this setting, a widely adopted method is to broadcast trajectory-level advantages to all sessions, but this does not distinguish contributions from various sessions or guide session allocation within trajectories. To address this issue, we propose Mosaic, a multi-session agentic RL method with critic-free hierarchical optimization. At the trajectory level, it incorporates session-usage signals into advantage estimation. At the session level, it shapes each session's advantage according to the estimated marginal contribution. Experiments on BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B show that Mosaic outperforms broadcasting in both context compaction and subagent forking scenarios while using fewer sessions on average. Further analyses show that our method achieves improvements in session utility and allocation, which we suggested is a promising target for future advances in multi-session agentic RL.

sections.content: Most existing agentic reinforcement learning methods assume single-session trajectories, where interaction proceeds within one continuously accumulated context. However, agentic techniques such as context compaction and subagent forking may produce trajectories spanning multiple sessions, creating mismatch between the single-session training assumption and inference-time execution. Therefore, we introduce Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, more general setting that supports an arbitrary number of sessions within trajectory. Under this setting, widely adopted method is to broadcast trajectory-level advantages to all sessions, but this does not distinguish contributions from various sessions or guide session allocation within trajectories. To address this issue, we propose Mosaic, multi-session agentic RL method with critic-free hierarchical optimization. At the trajectory level, it incorporates session-usage signals into advantage estimation. At the session level, it shapes each sessions advantage according to the estimated marginal contribution. Experiments on BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B show that Mosaic outperforms broadcasting in both context compaction and subagent forking scenarios while using fewer sessions on average. Further analyses show that our method achieves improvements in session utility and allocation, which we suggested is promising target for future advances in multi-session agentic RL. 1. Introduction Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL; Gao et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025) trains Large Language Model (LLM) agents (Shinn et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2022) for multi-turn reasoning, tool use, and interaction with external environments via online rollouts and reward feedback, yielding broad performance gains. More recently, LLM agents have incorporated advanced inference techniques, such as context management (Mei et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a) and harness engineering (Lin et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026), enabling agentic workflows to tackle increasingly complex and long-horizon tasks. However, most agentic RL methods assume single-session setting, where each rollout unfolds as coherent multi-turn trajectory within continuously accumulated context and yields single training segment (Wang et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026b). We argue that the single-session setting is not sufficiently general for optimizing LLM agents. For example, context compaction compresses the execution history to free up context space while rewriting the prefix that conditions subsequent actions (Lu et al., 2025; Nguyen et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025), thereby initiating new session. Similarly, subagent forking delegates global goal to subagents which creates branch sessions (Song et al., 2025; Team et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026d). Those resulting trajectories no longer satisfy the single-session assumption, creating mismatch between training and inference that compromises consistency and limits optimization potential. Corresponding author(s): Zhijiang Guo (zhijiangguo@hkust-gz.edu.cn), Haochen Tan (haochetan2-c@my.cityu.edu.hk) Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning Figure 1 The comparison between multi-session and single-session trajectories. To address this gap, we introduce new setting termed Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, which supports an arbitrary count of sessions and enables agents with diverse inference mechanisms to be optimized within unified algorithm. straightforward way to handle multi-session rollouts is through broadcasting, whereby trajectory-level outcome reward or advantage is replicated to every token across all sessions (Accio-Lab, 2026; Xu et al., 2026a). However, we argue that this method provides only coarse supervision and offers no explicit control over optimization across sessions, resulting in poorly targeted learning signals as trajectories span more sessions. In this work, we propose Mosaic, multi-session agentic RL method with critic-free hierarchical optimization. First, session-aware trajectory-level advantage estimation calibrates outcome-based advantages using within-group rankings of session counts conditioned on task outcomes, encouraging successful trajectories to solve tasks efficiently while allowing unsuccessful trajectories sufficient exploration. Its bounded modulation preserves outcome-induced ordering while incorporating sessionusage guidance, thereby widening relative advantage margins for homogeneous-reward groups. Second, session-level advantage shaping calculates each sessions marginal outcome gain as an immediate reward, applies group-relative normalization separately by session type, and combines the resulting shaping signal with the trajectory-level advantage. Overall, the former provides long-term, outcome-oriented global signal, while the latter captures short-term local marginal effects. They together form hierarchical optimization target for multi-session agentic RL. To evaluate our method, we conduct experiments on BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025) and select Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026) as the base model. Our Mosaic outperforms multiple single-session and multi-session agentic RL baselines under both context compaction and subagent forking scenarios. Moreover, Mosaic achieves up to 10.1% relative improvement in accuracy over the broadcasting baseline while using fewer sessions per trajectory on average (3.17 2.35). Ablation studies further demonstrate that session-aware trajectory-level advantage estimation and session-level advantage shaping each contribute to the final performance gains. Our analyses also reveal several key insights: (1) shaping trajectory-level advantages with session counts increases within-group advantage variance and improves sample efficiency; (2) different session types exhibit distinct distributions of session-level marginal gains, which our type-conditioned normalization helps stabilize; (3) effective multi-session optimization improves session utility and allocation, pattern that Mosaic strengthens and that might offer potential direction for future work. 2. Experiments 4.1. Experimental Setup Benchmark. We evaluate our method on BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025), challenging benchmark consisting of 1,266 questions that require agents to persistently navigate the web and identify hardto-find, entangled information. We select BrowseComp since its high difficulty demands long-horizon interactions, making it suitable for assessing agents that produce multi-session trajectories. Baselines. We use Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026) as the initial model and adopt ReAct-style agent loop. We organize the baselines by inference configuration. Under single-session inference, we evaluate (1) the initial model without RL training and (2) model trained with GRPO in the single-session setting, representing conventional Agentic RL. Under multi-session inference, we evaluate (3) the single-session GRPO trained model, representing test-time scaling; (4) model trained with Broadcasting in the multi-session setting; and (5) model trained with Mosaic in the multi-session setting. We evaluate all multi-session configurations under both context compaction and subagent forking using their respective agent loops; for multi-session training, the same loops are used to collect rollouts. Finally, since our session-level advantage shaping in 3.2 builds on information gain, we evaluate (6) single-session model trained with IGPO (Wang et al., 2026). 7 Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning Figure 3 (a). Percentage of the 972 tasks failed by the base model under single-session inference that are solved by different methods under multi-session inference with compact. (b). Comparison of the computation time for marginal information gain. (c)(d). Ablation results on BrowseComp. Implementation Details. The agent has two tools, search and visit, implemented using Serper 1 and Jina Reader 2 APIs, respectively. During training and evaluation, deepseek-v4-flash (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026) serves as the LLM judge for verifying final answers. For context compaction, the agent compresses its interaction history when approaching the context limit. For subagent forking, it can invoke non-nested subagents through dedicated action. Each session is limited to 128K tokens. For RL training, we use REDSearcher_RL_1k (Chu et al., 2026), which contains 1,000 challenging deep-search tasks. We train all models for one epoch with rollout batch size of 16 and group size of 8. We set 𝜌 = 0.2, 𝛽0 = 0.1, 𝛽1 = 0.2. and 𝜆𝑟 = 0.1. 4.2. RQ1: Overall Effectiveness of Mosaic RQ1 asks whether training in the multi-session setting improves agent performance and whether Mosaic contributes beyond broadcasting. As shown in Table 1, single-session inference has limited effectiveness on BrowseComp. Agentic RL training in the single-session setting yields modest gains, even when combined with test-time scaling in the multi-session setting. This suggests that multi-session inference capabilities do not readily emerge through generalization alone. Among methods trained on multi-session trajectories, Broadcasting improves multi-session inference performance. Mosaic improves it further, outperforming all baselines in both the compact and subagent scenarios. Figure 3 (a) illustrates the transformative gains from multi-session inference, multi-session training, and Mosaic. Figure 4 shows the training dynamics of each method. Mosaic boosts trajectory reward faster than Broadcasting and reaches higher level. The number of sessions increases over training for both methods, but its growth levels off more clearly with Mosaic. This may be partly due to the more targeted signal provided by its session-aware advantage, which discourages unnecessary increases in session count. Overall, Mosaic achieves better task performance at lower execution cost. As 3.2 applies marginal gain to session-level advantage shaping, we thus compare Mosaic with IGPO, which applies it at the turn level. From Table 1, Mosaic achieves better performance than IGPO. RQ2: Ablation Study of Mosaic RQ2 asks whether each component of Mosaic contributes to its overall performance. Figure 3 (c)(d) presents the ablation results. Relative to Broadcasting, both levels of components in Mosaic, namely trajectory-level session-aware advantage estimation and session-level advantage shaping, contribute to the enhanced final performance. Combining the two components yields clear additional gain in the compact scenario, but only modest gain in the subagent scenario. One possible explanation lies in their session structures: compact trajectories are linear, whereas subagent trajectories have nonlinear structure that more closely resembles directed acyclic graph. In the latter case, session may influence multiple succeeding sessions. Its immediate reward, estimated from marginal gain, may thus differ from its actual contribution to the final outcome. 4.4. RQ3: Mechanistic Analysis of Mosaic RQ3 asks how the design of Mosaic contributes to the training process. First, we examine whether session-aware trajectory-level advantage estimation produces the intended ordering. As shown in Figure 5, within mixed-outcome groups, advantages approximately decrease with session count for successful trajectories and increase for unsuccessful ones, while successful trajectories retain higher advantages. In homogeneous-outcome groups, the fallback mechanism introduces session-dependent variation, providing differentiated learning signals despite identical outcome rewards. These patterns illustrate how Mosaic leverages session signals to increase the within-group variance of relative advantages, thus improving sample efficiency during training. Second, we examine the effect of reward normalization on session-level shaping signals. As shown in Figure 5, the distributions of raw marginal information gain differ across session types, primarily because heterogeneous sessions serve distinct functions. Under global normalization, compaction sessions, whose raw marginal gains have lower mean, are further downweighted, introducing systematic bias against them. In Mosaic, type-conditioned normalization instead centers and rescales each type separately, enabling both types to receive positive and negative signals relative to their respective baselines. This reduces type-dependent distributional bias in advantage shaping. 4.5. However, the session count used by Mosaic serves only as proxy signal and is not inherently tied to exploration intensity or execution cost. Moreover, at inference time, the model has no access to hindsight: it does not know how many sessions trajectory will ultimately contain or whether the trajectory will succeed. Accordingly, we examine session-level behavior along three dimensions: quantity, or whether the count of sessions increases or decreases; quality, or whether performance improvement is accompanied by more useful sessions; and allocation, or whether limited session budget becomes increasingly concentrated on execution stages with high marginal utility. As shown in Table 2, for Broadcasting, which does not directly optimize any specific session-aware pattern, all three metrics increase. Under Mosaic, the number of sessions does not increase further, while both session quality and allocation improve. These findings indicate that performance gains via multi-session optimization are associated with improved session utility rather than monotonic rise in session count. Moreover, despite using explicit session-aware optimization, Mosaic does not induce fundamentally altered behavioral mechanism. Instead, it strengthens the session-allocation patterns that already emerge from naïve multi-session optimization. We argue that effective multi-session optimization is accompanied by improvements in session utility and allocation. It distributes computation more effectively across sessions, encouraging continued execution when it yields meaningful progress while suppressing low-utility computation. From this perspective, the central challenge is not how many sessions an agent should use, but how much useful progress it can derive from the sessions it executes. 5. Discussion: Future Directions for Multi-Session Agentic RL Infrastructure for reproducible research. Multi-session trajectories tend to arise naturally when agents tackle complex, long-horizon tasks. Although some existing benchmarks can elicit these trajectories with reasonable frequency, suitable public training data remain scarce. This gap limits the scale, sufficiency, and reproducibility of experiments in multi-session agentic RL. Developing open training datasets and corresponding agentic execution environments is therefore essential to building sustainable research ecosystem for this topic. 10 Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning Cross-session state transfer as central learning objective. Context compaction and subagent forking both involve information transfer, but serve different purposes: compaction must preserve sufficient working state for continued execution; forking must provide the information needed to complete subtask; merging must integrate subtask results into state usable by the main agent. These operations motivate shared research question: under limited context budget, what information should be carried forward to support subsequent decisions? CompactionRL already jointly optimizes task execution and context summarization (Li et al., 2026). unified approach to learning state transfer across compaction, forking, and merging remains an important direction, alongside systematic investigation of information loss and error accumulation over repeated transfers. Asynchronous training for multi-session rollouts. For partial rollout or asynchronous training settings, multi-session execution can amplify variation in trajectory lengths and completion times, increase policy staleness and complicate within-group comparisons and sample reuse. For instance, prioritizing completed rollouts may favor trajectories with less sessions over longer ones associated with harder tasks, introducing selection bias and shaping learned execution strategies. Our experiments use colocated setup with alternating rollout and training phases to minimize interference from asynchrony and isolate the effects of the optimization signals. Scaling toward actual production raises further question: how can multi-session optimization remain reliable under asynchronous sampling and policy staleness? SAO explores asynchronous optimization with one rollout per prompt, using learned value model (Hou et al., 2026). However, critic-free, group-relative optimization requires further investigation into when and how rollout groups are formed, how stale samples are handled, and how collected trajectories can be reused. Toward RL within (black-boxed) agent harnesses. General multi-session agentic RL can accommodate workflows in which execution no longer follows single, continuously accumulated context prefix. Context compaction and subagent forking, the two scenarios studied in this work, are representative examples of such workflows in modern agent harnesses. Progress in multi-session optimization could thus provide an important foundation for training agents within harnesses whose orchestration is partially opaque (Xu et al., 2026a), such as Claude Code. Therefore, critical next step is to systematically examine mechanisms across agent harnesses that disrupt context continuity, such as dropping reasoning tokens or tool responses, and improve general multi-session agentic RL under these conditions. Additionally, when discontinuity occurs, the choice between introducing new session boundary and applying lossy concatenation with the preceding session may also influence the overall effectiveness of optimization. 6. Related Work LLM Agents. LLM agents extend LLMs with tool use and environment interaction to work autonomously (Feng et al., 2026; Li et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2026). ReAct constructs general agent loop of reasoning, acting, observing environment feedback, and continuing until task completion (Yao et al., 2022). To handle complex and long-horizon tasks, recent systems develop agent harnesses that manage execution beyond the basic ReAct loop (OpenClaw, 2026; Works, 2026), incorporating context compaction (Nguyen et al., 2025), multi-agent system (Chen et al., 2026a), subagent forking (Team et al., 2026), and other forms of context and workflow management (Chen et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026c; Yang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). 11 Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning Agentic RL. Reinforcement learning techniques such as RLHF (Ouyang et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2026b) and RLVR (Chen et al., 2026b; Yu et al., 2026) are used to improve LLMs alignment, reasoning, and downstream task-solving capabilities (Tan et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025). Agentic RL extends this paradigm to LLM agents, aiming to enhance capabilities of multi-turn interaction through enhanced rollout sampling (Dong et al., 2026; Hou et al., 2025), process-level reward design (Liu et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c), and other optimization strategies (Deng et al., 2026). However, most existing agentic RL methods still assume that each trajectory is contained within single session. 7. Conclusion In this paper, we first identify mismatch between the single-session assumption underlying most existing agentic RL methods and advanced agentic inference techniques such as context compaction and subagent forking. This motivates our formulation of Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, which supports an arbitrary count of sessions within trajectory. To address the coarse supervision issue existed in the currently widely used broadcasting approach, we further propose Mosaic, multi-session agentic RL method with critic-free hierarchical optimization. By combining sessionaware trajectory-level advantage estimation with session-level advantage shaping, Mosaic trains Qwen3.5-4B agent that outperforms both single-session and multi-session baselines on BrowseComp. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component, while further analyses suggest that effective multi-session optimization might depend on improving session utility and allocation, pattern observed in both broadcasting baseline and our Mosaic. We hope these findings will inform future research on multi-session agentic RL. 12 Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning
